## Welcome{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
The **MSDM Culminating Experience Project (CEP)** 

-  The capstone of your graduate journey — a year-long applied project where you put everything you have learned to work on a real digital marketing challenge.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
This session covers what you need to know **before the project begins**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .accent-box}
Today's agenda: What is the CEP → Timeline → Proposals → Choosing a project → PO vs. AO → Individual accountability → Project management → Pitfalls to avoid
:::

---

## What Is the CEP?{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Spans **one full academic year** — Fall, Spring, Summer
- Groups of **4–6 students** per project
- One **Faculty Lead** (committee chair) per project
- Produces: analysis, insights, a **digital marketing plan**, and campaign execution
- Assessed against MSDM **Student Learning Outcomes (SLOs)**
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.accent-box}
**Two completion pathways**

- **2-year roadmap**: CEP begins Fall of Year 2
- **1-year accelerated**: CEP begins Fall of Year 1
:::
:::

::::

- Projects aligned with research interests or industry connections
- Already have domain expertise to guide students

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Students
- Projects tied to your employer or industry connections

**Businesses and organizations** can be involved as clients, but the proposal must be submitted by a faculty member or a student with a committed faculty lead.

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.incremental}

3. **Student-initiated project for a client** — student brings the idea and client connection; faculty lead required

::: {.fragment .fade-in .accent-box}

# Project Objectives vs. Analytics Objectives {background-color="#154734"}

::: {.divider-sub}
The most important distinction in the entire CEP process
:::

---

## Why This Distinction Matters{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fade-in}
- Clients express their needs as **business goals** — things they want to achieve. These are **Project Objectives (PO)**.
:::

::: {.fade-in}
- But the CEP requires **data analysis** — and analysis requires objectives that are directly tied to data. These are **Analytics Objectives (AO)**.
:::

::: {.fade-in .warn-box}
Students who cannot tell the difference will not make informed decisions — and may discover in Spring that they have **nothing to analyze in Chapter 4**.
:::

---

## PO vs. AO — The Core Test{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

Ask yourself two diagnostic questions:

::: {.incremental}
1. **"Is there data associated with this objective?"** — If no, it is a PO, not an AO.
2. **"What statistical method would I use to address this in Chapter 3?"** — If you cannot name a method, it is a PO.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
### Example
> *"Design an effective website that will promote the new service and generate leads."*

Is there a statistical method required to design a website? **No** — designing a website is a project activity. Thus, this is a **PO**.
:::

---

## How to Convert PO to AO{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

Ask the guiding question:

> **"What information do I need, and where can I find it, in order to achieve the project objectives?"**

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**PO1**: Design a website to engage potential clients and increase conversion rates.

↓ Collect GA4 data: bounce rate, session duration, conversion rate, visitors

↓ Ask: what does the data tell us? What improves engagement?
:::

<hr style="border: 1px solid #B08D57; margin: 0.6em 0;">

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**AO1a**: Explore ways in which the website can be optimized for potential customers.

**AO1b**: Generate insights from GA4 and Google Ads data for website optimization.

**AO1c**: Generate insights from GA4 and Google Ads data to increase visitor engagement and conversions.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .accent-box}
Choose the AO statement that is **clearest and most concrete**. AO1c wins here.
:::

---

## One AO Per Person{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- Each group member (4–6 students) owns **exactly one Analytics Objective** — from proposal through data collection, analysis, and report writing.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- This is what makes individual performance measurable in a group project.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
<table>
<thead><tr><th>Group size</th><th>Number of AOs</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>4 students</td><td>4 AOs (one each)</td></tr>
<tr><td>5 students</td><td>5 AOs (one each)</td></tr>
<tr><td>6 students</td><td>6 AOs (one each)</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .accent-box}
Your AO is **your analytical responsibility** — you design the method, collect the data, run the analysis, and write Chapter 4 for it.
:::

---

# Individual Accountability {background-color="#154734"}

::: {.divider-sub}
How individual performance is documented and graded
:::

---

## How Individual Contributions Are Tracked{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.incremental}
1. **One AO per person** — each student is individually responsible for their analytics objective throughout the year
2. **Shared cloud folder with subfolders per person** — each member has their own named subfolder in OneDrive, creating transparent, documented contributions
3. **Individual Contribution Statement (ICS)** — required at the end of the project; each student writes their own, submitted to the library as part of graduation paperwork
4. **Faculty Lead assessment at each milestone** — your faculty lead formally evaluates individual performance at W09, W15, and again in Spring and Summer; course instructors use those evaluations for grades
:::

---

## The Individual Contribution Statement{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
The ICS is submitted at the end of Summer (W10) as part of the final paperwork package.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
It documents:

- What specific work **you personally** contributed to the project
- Which AO was yours and how you addressed it
- Your role in data collection, analysis, writing, and presentation
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .accent-box}
**The ICS is not a group document.** Each member writes their own and it is submitted individually to the library via Bronco ScholarWorks.
:::

---

# Project Management {background-color="#154734"}

::: {.divider-sub}
Collaboration expectations with your group, faculty lead, and client
:::

---

## Working with Your Group{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.incremental}
- **Create a shared OneDrive folder** — give edit access to all members and your faculty lead (the whole folder, not just selected files)
- **Use a shared agenda for meetings** — Google Docs or Word with Navigation Pane; update it before each meeting
- **Create subfolders with each person's name** — transparency prevents free-riding and reduces conflict
- **Establish Zotero Web Library for group for literature review** — share references and notes; faculty lead can see your progress
- **Create GitHub Repository for code and output** — share code, scripts, and results; group members and faculty lead can see your progress
- **Hold a group meeting before each faculty meeting** — align internally, assign tasks, prepare questions
- **Use a project management tool** — Notion is recommended; helps track tasks, milestones, and deadlines
:::

---

## Meeting Frequency — Faculty Lead{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Meet with your faculty lead **once every other week** — unless there is no agenda
- Share **written agenda before the meeting** — especially if you want the faculty lead to prepare
- Send a **calendar invitation** to all attendees for every meeting
- Use a **recurring invite** with a shared cloud document for agendas — update it before each meeting
- If skipping a week, send a **brief update email** instead
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.accent-box}
**When faculty engagement is highest**

Faculty leads need at least **one hour per every other week** to review your work and provide technical guidance. Their involvement is most critical during **data collection and data analysis**.
:::
:::

::::

---

## Meeting Frequency — Client{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.incremental}
- Client meetings are **less frequent** than faculty meetings
- Invite the client only when their input is **genuinely required**:
  - Company background or data not publicly available
  - Approval, resources, or cooperation requests
  - All major required presentations (Fall W09, W15; Spring W06, W13, W16; Summer W05, W09)
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .warn-box}
**Do not invite the client to every meeting with the faculty lead.** They are busy. They do not need to observe your internal working sessions with your faculty lead. This is a consulting project, not an internship — present your best work.
:::

---

## Best Scheduling Practices{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- Use a **recurring calendar invite** for biweekly faculty meetings
- Include the meeting agenda (or link to it) in the invite
- If the agenda changes, update the shared cloud document — not the invite itself
- Cancel or reschedule **only the specific instance**, not the entire series
- Always notify participants through the calendar system
:::
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.accent-box}
**Recommended tools**

- **Agenda management**: Google Docs tabs or Word with Navigation Pane
- **Project tracking**: Notion
- **File sharing**: OneDrive (Cal Poly Pomona supported)
- **Scheduling**: Outlook calendar with recurring invite
- **Code sharing**: GitHub
- **Reference management**: Zotero Web Library
- **Report Writing**: Quarto or Word
- **Presentation**: Quarto or PowerPoint
:::
:::

::::

# Pitfalls to Avoid {background-color="#154734"}

::: {.divider-sub}
Six common mistakes that derail CEP projects
:::

---

## Pitfall 1 — Confusing PO with AO{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
This is the **most common and most consequential** mistake. Students who cannot tell the difference design a project they cannot analyze.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .warn-box}
If your AO is actually a PO, you will arrive at **Chapter 4 with nothing to analyze** — and Chapter 4 is the entire Spring semester.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Check every objective** using the two diagnostic questions:

1. Is there data associated with this objective?
2. What statistical method would I use in Chapter 3?

If you cannot answer both — it is a PO. Convert it.
:::

---

## Pitfall 2 — No Data by Fall W15{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- Data is the lifeblood of your spring semester. Without it, you cannot analyze, you cannot write Chapter 4, and you cannot create a data-informed marketing plan.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- Students without solid data at the W15 defense will receive a **temporary grade (I or RP)** for IBM 6500. Remediation happens during winter break.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .warn-box}
**Winter break goes quickly.** Most people take a break in mid-December through early January. Do not count on making serious progress during break — get your data in the fall.
:::

---

## Pitfall 3 — Poor Project Management{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.incremental}
- **Not scheduling weekly meetings early** — establish your recurring faculty meeting cadence by Week 4 at the latest
- **Waiting until the deadline to flag problems** — if your data plan hits a barrier, tell your faculty lead immediately, not the week before W15
- **No shared agenda** — meetings without a pre-shared agenda waste the faculty lead's time and your own
- **Not using a project management tool** — tasks fall through the cracks; milestones are missed; team members lose track of who owns what
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .accent-box}
Treat your faculty lead like a consulting client — come prepared, communicate proactively, and respect their time.
:::

---

## Pitfall 4 — Inviting the Client to Every Meeting{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- Clients are **extremely busy**. They are not interested in observing your internal working process.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- Inviting the client too often has three downsides:

  1. Limits the time your faculty lead can spend guiding you — they hold back in front of the client
  2. Exposes your "working kitchen" — the client should see polished work, not rough drafts
  3. Signals that you cannot self-manage — this is a consulting engagement, not an internship
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .accent-box}
Invite the client **purposefully** — when you need their information, approval, or attendance at a required milestone presentation.
:::

---

## Pitfall 5 — Waiting Until Spring to Secure Data{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Spring Day 1 = analysis begins. There is no time in spring to collect or clean data.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- **If you are using GA4 data:** GA4 must be set up and tracking in the fall so you accumulate at least one month of data before W15. Infrastructure (GA4 + GTM + UTM) setup starts at W04.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- **If you are doing survey research:** IRB approval takes 2–3 weeks minimum. Apply at W10. Data collection cannot begin until approval is granted.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .warn-box}
**Secondary data is not automatically ready either.** Confirm data integrity (variables, completeness, access) during the fall. Missing variables discovered in spring = a failed analytics objective.
:::

---

## Pitfall 6 — Missing the Summer W09 Presentation{.unnumbered}

<div class="cpp-rule"></div>

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
The Summer Week 9 final presentation is the one milestone explicitly tied to **graduation eligibility**.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .warn-box}
- **Failure to complete this presentation = inability to graduate at the end of summer.** There is no make-up. There is no extension. Plan for this from Day 1.
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
Why it matters:

- W10 requires final edits and committee signatures via Adobe Docu
- W11 requires RCE submission by your faculty lead + abstract submission to library
- These administrative steps take time — you cannot compress them

Start your campaign early (ideally end of Spring) so you have enough performance data to assess by W09.
:::
